summary: Manufacturer Usage Description (MUD) lets device makers tell the network what an IoT device should do. This RFC extends MUD so manufacturers can describe expected TLS and DTLS parameters. A network security service can then spot unexpected encryption behavior that might signal malware or unauthorized software.

eli5.summary: A toy's box says how it should talk to the internet. If it starts talking differently, the network can notice that something may be wrong.

questions: how to detect unexpected tls use by iot devices
how does a firewall detect malware in tls
what yang modules does rfc 9761 define
can a firewall inspect tls 1.3 handshakes
subtitle: Lets IoT makers publish the TLS and DTLS behavior their devices should show, so networks can spot impostors.

tldr.problem: Malware on IoT devices increasingly hides inside encrypted (D)TLS traffic, and the Layer 3 and 4 access lists in MUD cannot tell intended encrypted use from malicious use.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds YANG modules that let a MUD file list a device's expected (D)TLS parameters, such as versions, cipher suites and extensions, which a firewall can compare against what it observes in handshakes.
tldr.outcome: A network security service can flag or block unexpected (D)TLS use, but visibility is partial in (D)TLS 1.3 because most of the handshake is encrypted.

today: RFC 9761 is a Proposed Standard from April 2025. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it is the current definition of MUD (D)TLS profiles. It builds on RFC 8520.

sections.title: Why Describe (D)TLS in a MUD File
sections.content:
TLS and DTLS, together written (D)TLS, are the dominant protocols encrypting IoT traffic. Malware authors use encryption too, which defeats deep packet inspection. The RFC lists patterns that set malware apart: older and weaker cryptographic parameters, server names that look generated by a domain generation algorithm, more self-signed certificates, mismatches between the SNI and the certificate's SubjectAltName, lower diversity of client extensions, ClientHello randomization, and using an alternative DNS server over an encrypted transport.

If a device's expected (D)TLS profile is known, a network can permit intended use and block malicious use. The RFC calls this better than the Layer 3 and 4 ACLs in RFC 8520 for broad communication patterns, and it is meant to complement the existing MUD specification, not replace it. The technique also suits deployments where decryption is undesirable because of privacy concerns, non-cooperating endpoints or cost.
sections.eli5: Bad programs hide their chatter inside secret code. If you know exactly how the real toy should talk, anything that talks differently stands out.

sections.title: How the Idea Works in Practice
sections.content:
Endpoint security agents may not be practical on IoT devices, so the network does the protecting. A middlebox need not proxy (D)TLS. It can passively watch handshakes, gaining visibility into TLS 1.2 parameters and partial visibility into TLS 1.3 parameters.

The RFC argues that malware has a hard time imitating many device types, models and manufacturers, and that its command and control server certificates must be signed by the same certificate authorities the device trusts. For devices at end of life, the is-supported attribute of RFC 8520 can tell the MUD manager that the maker no longer supports the device, and other techniques must then be used until it is replaced.
sections.eli5: A guard at the door does not open your letters. They just check that the envelope looks like the ones your toy usually sends.

sections.title: What a Middlebox Can See in (D)TLS 1.3
sections.content:
In (D)TLS 1.3 every handshake message except the ClientHello is encrypted, so the server certificate is hidden. The ClientHello and ServerHello still expose some fields: supported versions, named groups, cipher suites, signature algorithms, the extensions in the ClientHello, and the cipher chosen in the ServerHello. So a randomized ClientHello will not match the legitimate client's offered lists, and a middlebox can block it without acting as a proxy.

For more visibility, a middlebox can act as a (D)TLS 1.3 proxy for devices an enterprise owns and manages, following Section 9.3 of RFC 8446. Encrypted Client Hello hides the SNI and ALPN from passive observers, and a proxy that does not support ECH signals the client to disable it. A device pre-configured to use a DNS resolver not signaled by the network is generally incompatible with MUD, so a network-designated DoH/DoT server is needed, for example via RFC 9463 and RFC 9462.
sections.eli5: Most of the secret handshake is in a sealed envelope. Only the outside of the first message can be read, but that already says a lot.

sections.title: The (D)TLS Profile Data Model
sections.content:
The RFC defines three YANG modules. ietf-acl-tls augments the ACL model of RFC 8519 with a client-profiles container holding a list of tls-dtls-profile entries, each keyed by a name of 1 to 64 characters. iana-tls-profile holds the types and enumerations from IANA registries. ietf-mud-tls adds a boolean is-tls-dtls-profile-supported to the MUD container, defaulting to false.

A profile can list the following:

  • Supported TLS and DTLS versions.
  • Cipher suites and extension types.
  • Trust anchor certificates the device uses, so the middlebox can reject servers the device would not trust.
  • Pre-shared key exchange modes, supported groups and signature algorithms.
  • Application protocols, certificate compression algorithms and acceptable certificate authority names.

Profiles MUST NOT include GREASE values (RFC 8701). They also leave out compression methods, since only the null method is allowed in TLS 1.3.
sections.eli5: The profile is a checklist on the toy's box: which languages it speaks, which secret codes it knows and which guards it trusts.

sections.title: How a Firewall Processes a Profile
sections.content:
The processing rules are written so that the system does not ossify, meaning get stuck unable to accept new parameters.

  • A parameter that is seen, not in the profile and recognized by the firewall is unexpected use. The firewall can block the session or raise an alert.
  • A parameter that is not in the profile and not recognized is ignored by the firewall, and the correct behavior is not to block the session, as in Section 9.3 of RFC 8446. This also lets it ignore GREASE values.
  • If the profile lists a newer parameter the firewall does not recognize, an alert should go to the firewall vendor and the device owner, so the firewall must be readily updatable.
  • If the profile includes weak parameters, an alert MUST be triggered.

Section 7 gives an example MUD file for a device using TCP port 443 with TLS 1.3, cipher suites 4865 and 4866, extension types 10,11,13,16,24 and group 29. Cipher suites are written in decimal.
sections.eli5: If the toy does something its box forbids, the guard raises an alarm. If the guard simply does not know a word, it lets it pass and calls for a better dictionary.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Limits
sections.content:
The RFC admits that malware can still copy a legitimate profile. Parameters such as certificate authorities are hard to mimic, while signature algorithms are easier. Network security services should also use contextual data such as domain names and IP reputation, and anomaly detection. Effectiveness in (D)TLS 1.3 flows is much lower without contextual data or a proxy. The middlebox MUST follow the invariants of Section 9.3 of RFC 8446 to act as a compliant proxy.

The YANG modules have the usual NETCONF and RESTCONF considerations, and NACM default-deny-write is set on the data nodes. On privacy, the MUD URL MUST be encrypted and shared only with authorized components so an on-path attacker cannot identify the device. Full handshake inspection needs a proxy that decrypts traffic, and the RFC says use of (D)TLS proxies is NOT RECOMMENDED whenever possible.
sections.eli5: A clever thief might copy the toy's look, so the guard also checks other clues. And peeking inside every envelope is discouraged because it invades privacy.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content: IANA has registered the three YANG modules and created an IANA-maintained iana-tls-profile module. It created three registries: ACL TLS Version Codes (1 for tls12, 2 for tls13), ACL DTLS Version Codes (1 for dtls12, 2 for dtls13) and ACL (D)TLS Parameters. New entries use Expert Review, and the experts must ensure the version or parameter is one standardized by the IETF. IANA also created the MUD Extension name ietf-mud-tls.
sections.eli5: A public list is kept of which codes mean which versions, so every box and every guard uses the same words.
